procedural_history.impugned_order: Summoning Order dated 08.03.2021 by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Aligarh in Case No.129/2020 (corrected to Case No. 5727/2021) under Sections 147, 342, 323, 307, 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, Police Station, Civil Lines, District Aligarh. This order took cognizance of the offenses and summoned the accused (appellant).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant assailed the CJM's order before the Allahabad High Court by way of a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. registered as Application u/s.482 No.15273 of 2021. The High Court dismissed this application on 24.08.2021.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court because the Allahabad High Court dismissed their application to quash the CJM's summoning order. The Supreme Court is hearing an appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 2134 of 2024) against the High Court's order.

directions: Impugned orders passed by the High Court and also the CJM are set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) and the High Court erred in taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) by relying not only on the Protest Petition but also on the affidavits of witnesses filed along with it, instead of following the procedure for a complaint case.

facts: Following an FIR, the police conducted an investigation and filed a closure report under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., stating that no evidence was found to substantiate the allegations.
The original complainant filed a 'Protest Petition' against this closure report.
Along with the Protest Petition, the complainant also submitted their own affidavit and the affidavits of four other witnesses as additional evidence.
The Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) rejected the police's closure report and took cognizance of the offence under Section 190(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C.

The CJM's decision to take cognizance was explicitly based not just on the police report materials, but also on the Protest Petition and the additional witness affidavits, which he believed made out a prima facie case and showed the police investigation was not fair.
law: When a police closure report is filed, a Magistrate has several options.

One option is to disagree with the police and take cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C. This must be based on the material collected by the police during the investigation (the case diary). A Protest Petition can be used to draw the Magistrate's attention to this material.

Another option is to treat the Protest Petition as a private complaint. If the Magistrate chooses this path, especially when relying on new evidence submitted by the complainant (like witness affidavits), they must take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) Cr.P.C.

When taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) based on a complaint, the Magistrate is required to follow the procedure under Chapter XV of the Cr.P.C., which includes examining the complainant and their witnesses on oath under Section 200.
application: The Supreme Court found that the CJM did not merely use the Protest Petition to re-examine the police's case diary. Instead, the CJM explicitly relied on the new evidence submitted with the petition—the affidavits of the complainant and four witnesses.
By relying on this additional material, which was outside the scope of the police investigation report, the CJM was effectively treating the Protest Petition as a complaint.
Therefore, the correct legal procedure was to take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) Cr.P.C. and follow the mandatory steps for a complaint case as laid out in Chapter XV (Sections 200 and 202).

The CJM committed a procedural error by taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b), which is reserved for cases based on a police report, while simultaneously relying on evidence from a private complaint.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the CJM and the High Court erred. Once the Magistrate decided to rely on the additional evidence (witness affidavits) filed with the Protest Petition, he could not take cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C. The only proper course of action was to treat the Protest Petition as a complaint, take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a), and follow the procedure prescribed for complaint cases. The Court, therefore, accepted the appellant's argument and left it open for the Magistrate to now treat the petition as a complaint and proceed according to law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) and the High Court erred in taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) by relying not only on the Protest Petition but also on the affidavits of witnesses filed along with it, instead of following the procedure for a complaint case.
appellant_arguments: The CJM and the High Court erred in taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C. because the CJM relied not only on the Protest Petition but also on the affidavits of witnesses filed with it.

When a magistrate relies on additional material and evidence filed by the complainant along with a Protest Petition, the only option is to treat it as a complaint under Section 200 Cr.P.C. and follow the procedure for a private complaint case.
The case should have been treated as a private complaint under Chapter XV of the Cr.P.C. and not continued as a State case.

While the CJM could have rejected the police closure report and taken cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) by relying solely on the material collected during the investigation (the case diary), the use of additional evidence mandated taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) as a private complaint.
respondent_arguments: The CJM did not take into consideration any additional evidence, such as the affidavits filed with the Protest Petition.
The CJM only relied upon the material collected during the investigation as contained in the case diary.
The decision to reject the police report and take cognizance was based solely on the material in the case diary, which is within the magistrate's domain.
Consequently, the cognizance correctly falls under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C., and the impugned order does not suffer from any infirmity.

cases.case_name: Vishnu Kumar Tiwari v. State of Uttar Pradesh, through Secretary Home, Civil Secretariat, Lucknow & Anr.
cases.principle: Regarding the procedural options available to a Magistrate when a protest petition is filed. If the Magistrate treats the protest petition as a complaint, the procedure under Sections 200 and 202 of the CrPC (examining the complainant and witnesses) must be followed. Alternatively, if the material in the protest petition persuades the court to disagree with the investigating officer's conclusions, cognizance can be taken under Section 190(1)(b) without the need to examine witnesses under Section 200.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate is not compelled to treat a protest petition as a complaint. If the Magistrate disagrees with the conclusions in a police final report, they can take cognizance of an offence under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure based on the materials submitted with the report, without needing to examine witnesses under Section 200. However, if the Magistrate chooses to treat the protest petition as a complaint, they must follow the procedure prescribed under Sections 200 and 202 of the Code, which includes examining the complainant and their witnesses.
obiter: If a Magistrate is not compelled to treat a protest petition as a complaint, the remedy for the complainant is to file a fresh complaint and invite the Magistrate to follow the procedure under Section 200 or Section 200 read with Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) erred by taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. because he did not rely solely on the police report and case diary. Instead, the CJM explicitly considered the Protest Petition and, crucially, the affidavits of witnesses filed along with it to conclude that a prima facie case was made out. Once the Magistrate relied on this additional evidence provided by the complainant, he was legally obligated to treat the Protest Petition as a complaint and follow the distinct procedure prescribed under Chapter XV of the Cr.P.C. (i.e., Sections 200 and 202), which he failed to do.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a Magistrate, when disagreeing with a police closure report, is taking cognizance based solely on the materials collected during the investigation (which falls under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C.), or is also relying on additional materials and evidence submitted by the complainant with a Protest Petition.

If the Magistrate relies on additional materials like affidavits submitted with a Protest Petition to form a prima facie view, the matter must be treated as a complaint under Section 190(1)(a) Cr.P.C., and the procedure under Chapter XV (Sections 200 and 202) must be followed.
why_respondent_won: The court factually determined that the CJM's order was not based solely on the police report, but on the Protest Petition and the accompanying affidavits of witnesses. The court held: 'The CJM had actually taken into consideration not only the Protest Petition but also the affidavit filed in support of the Protest Petition as well as the four affidavits of witnesses filed along with the Protest Petition'.

The court ruled that once the CJM relied on these external affidavits to form his opinion, the only legally correct path was to treat the matter as a complaint case. The court concluded: '...this Court is of the view that the Magistrate ought to have followed the provisions and the procedure prescribed under Chapter XV of the Cr.P.C.'
By taking cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) after considering evidence outside the police record, the CJM committed a procedural error that vitiated the order.
policy_considerations: The judgment reinforces the strict procedural distinction between initiating a case based on a police report versus a private complaint. When a court relies on evidence provided by a private party (like affidavits with a protest petition), it must follow the specific procedural safeguards for complaint cases, such as examining the complainant and witnesses on oath under Section 200 Cr.P.C., to ensure the threshold for proceeding is met fairly and transparently.
